Saturday, 6 December 2036. In La Duchère, a new media library named after Hortense Valmont’s mother is being opened. The academician has come from Paris. Sami introduces her to Haruka, who complains that she reads too slowly.
I understand everything I read. But I read too slowly. In the mock exam, I didn’t have time to finish the second text.
I bet you translate every word in your head.
Yes. And when I don’t know a word, I look it up in the dictionary.
In the exam you won’t have a dictionary. You have to learn to guess. The context almost always tells you what the word means.
Madame Valmont, you’re the one saying that? You, who have spent your life in dictionaries?
(she smiles) Precisely. I know what they’re worth. A good reader first skims: the title, the first sentence of each paragraph, the conclusion.
Then you look for the thesis: what the author wants you to think. Then the arguments, which are announced by connectors: “first”, “moreover”, “however”, “consequently”.
Connectors are like the skeleton of the text. If you find them, you have the whole plan.
And the “true or false” questions? I often get them wrong.
Because you answer with your opinion. You have to answer with the text, and copy out the exact sentence that proves it. No more, no less.
Read between the lines, but justify with the lines.
Mademoiselle, I’m going to steal that sentence for my next speech.
The paper lasts one hour and is marked out of 25. You get two authentic texts:
the main information and the details
the thesis, the arguments, the author’s position
Split your time: about 25 minutes per text and 10 minutes for checking. Don’t get stuck on one question.
Before reading carefully, map the text in 2–3 minutes:
the title and the standfirst (the introductory paragraph in bold)
the first sentence of each paragraph (it usually announces the idea)
the conclusion (it often repeats the thesis)
the questions (they tell you what to look for)
Typical mistake: reading the first text word by word, with a dictionary in your head. You lose time for the second text, which is usually harder.

An argumentative text often begins with the opposing opinion (“Certains pensent que…”) only to reject it (“Pourtant…”). The thesis comes after “pourtant”, not before!
When you don’t know a word, you have four tools:
the word family: “illisible” comes from “lire” → that cannot be read
context: after ten hours’ work → “épuisé” = exhausted
transparent words: they look like English or other languages you know
Watch out for “false friends”: “librairie” = bookshop (not library), “location” = rental, “sensible” = sensitive (not reasonable), “rester” = to stay (not to rest).

Haruka had always believed reading would be the easiest paper. She had been reading French for three years, had devoured dozens of novels, and understood almost everything she read. At the first reading mock exam, at the end of November, she sat down confidently, pencil in hand — Odile’s pencil. She read the first text slowly, attentively, sentence by sentence. She understood everything.

Then she looked up at the clock. Eighteen minutes left. The second text was two pages long, with twelve questions. She began reading faster, then faster still, skipping lines, panicking. When the invigilator announced the end of the paper, she had answered only four of the twelve questions. She got fourteen out of twenty-five. Not low enough to be eliminated. Not high enough to feel safe.

The exam would take place on Saturday 13 December at the Alliance française, in the same room as the mock exams. In the morning, the three group papers: listening, reading, writing. In the afternoon, the oral, face to face with two examiners. Four papers, a hundred points, and you needed fifty to pass, with at least five in each paper. Haruka had copied these numbers onto a sheet she stuck above her bed, next to Bernard’s record.

That evening she told Isabelle about it, sitting in Odile’s armchair with her notebook on her knees. Isabelle had been a publisher for thirty years. She had read thousands of manuscripts, often bad ones, and could recognise a good book in ten minutes. She asked Haruka how she read. Haruka explained: word by word, translating each sentence into Japanese in her head, to be sure she missed nothing. Isabelle sighed. She said that was exactly the problem.

She explained that in the exam you weren’t asked to understand everything. You were asked to understand what mattered. Ideas, not words. Structure, not details. She said a publisher never read a manuscript from beginning to end the first time. They skimmed it, looking for the voice, the plan, the intention. Haruka asked how you learnt to do that. Isabelle said she knew someone who did it better than she did.

Isabelle also told her a story she had never told anyone. In 1998 she had turned down a manuscript after skimming it for ten minutes one evening when she was tired. The book was published by another house and sold two million copies. She told Haruka that reading fast was an art, but reading too fast was a risk. You had to know both: fly over first, then land where it mattered. Haruka wrote: “Fly over, then land.”

That someone was Hortense Valmont. The academician was coming to Lyon the following week. A new media library was to be opened in La Duchère, on the very spot where the long block she grew up in once stood. The city had decided to name it after Hortense’s mother, Jeanne Valmont, a seamstress who had raised four children on the seventh floor, who said “bagnole” and “boulot”, and who had taught herself to read at thirty, using her children’s books.

Hortense had never told this story in public. She had told it to Sami in the spring, in her office at the Académie, and Sami had told the mayor of Lyon, who had come up with the idea of the name. When Hortense heard, she refused at first. She said her mother would have hated having her name given to an official building. Then she thought it over. She said her mother would have hated the official building, but she would have adored the books. She accepted.

Hortense arrived at Part-Dieu station on Friday evening. Sami was waiting on the platform. She refused a taxi. She wanted to go up to La Duchère by bus, as she had at fifteen on her way to school. On the bus she looked out of the window without speaking, recognising streets, crossroads, a bakery that still existed. She told Sami it was the bakery where her mother bought bread on Sundays, when there was enough money left for a cake.

The opening took place on Saturday 6 December, on a cold, bright morning. The Jeanne-Valmont media library was a building of wood and glass set in the middle of the park, next to the old lime tree Rose-Hélène had been watering for years. Inside there were forty thousand books, a music room, a children’s corner with cushions on the floor, and big windows looking out at the tower blocks. Sami had asked for the music room to be named after the waltz. It was called the “Eight Bars Room”.

At the entrance to the media library, under glass, there was a photo of Jeanne Valmont. A small woman with grey hair pulled back, sitting at a kitchen table, a book open in front of her and round glasses on her nose. Next to the photo were the glasses themselves, the real ones, which Hortense had kept for fifty years in a drawer in her Paris office. She had brought them for the occasion. She said her mother had at last found a library to her measure.

There were a lot of people. Local residents, councillors, journalists, children running between the shelves. Leïla, Sami’s mother, had made honey cakes for three hundred people. Hortense arrived with her silver-handled cane and her grey suit. She was eighty-two. Getting out of the car, she stood for a long time in front of the building without a word. Then she pointed with the tip of her cane to a spot in the sky above the trees. She said: “It was there. The seventh floor.”

Mrs Roux, who was ninety, had come too, in her blue dress, on Isabelle’s arm. She had known Jeanne Valmont. They had worked together in the same sewing workshop near the Place Sathonay in 1962. She told Hortense that her mother used to hide a book under her sewing machine and read a page every time the forewoman turned her back. Hortense hadn’t known. She took Mrs Roux’s hand and didn’t let go of it for the rest of the ceremony.

She gave a short speech, without notes. She spoke of her mother, who read in the evenings by the kitchen light, following the lines with her finger and moving her lips. Who was ashamed of reading so slowly. Who said a book was a door, and it took courage to open it when you came from where she came from. She said this media library was the door her mother had never had. Then she cut the ribbon with scissors Leïla had lent her.

During the ceremony Henri-Ion had disappeared. He was found in the children’s corner, sitting on a cushion, reading a picture book to Awa, who was in her baby carrier beside him. Henri-Ion couldn’t read yet. He was making up the story from the pictures, with great confidence, and Awa listened with her big serious eyes. Hortense stopped to watch them. She said that was exactly how her mother had learnt to read: by making things up first.

After the ceremony, Sami introduced Haruka to Hortense. Haruka was intimidated. She bowed deeply, Japanese-style, which greatly pleased the academician. Hortense asked how she could help. Haruka explained her problem: she understood everything she read, but she read too slowly. She translated everything. She looked up every unknown word. In the exam she hadn’t had time to finish. Hortense listened closely, her head tilted to one side.

Haruka got her first library card that day. The librarian asked which book she wanted to borrow first. Haruka searched the shelves and came back with Camus’s “L’Étranger”. She had read it in Japanese at university. The librarian smiled. So did Haruka. She said it was the only book in the library about her, since she was the stranger. Then she added, laughing, that she hoped her own story would end better.

Then Hortense laughed. She said she had spent sixty years reading the way Haruka did, and that was why she had become a lexicographer. But in the exam you had to do exactly the opposite. Read like a bird flying over a landscape before landing. She took a book from the nearest shelf at random and opened it at any page. She asked Haruka to tell her, in thirty seconds, what the page was about.

Haruka began reading the first line carefully. Hortense shut the book under her nose after thirty seconds. Haruka had read only three lines. Hortense opened the book again at the same page. She said: “Now don’t read. Look. The first word of each paragraph. The capitalised words. The numbers. The verbs.” Haruka looked. After thirty seconds she said the page was about a train journey, in winter, between Paris and Marseille, with an argument. Hortense smiled. It was correct.

Hortense told her an anecdote about false friends. In the nineties, a British minister visiting Paris had wanted to compliment a French minister on her excellent work. He said she was “très sensible”, thinking he was saying “very sensible”. The minister took the compliment badly. Hortense said false friends were the most dangerous words in every language, because you thought you understood them. With real unknowns, at least, you knew you didn’t know them.

They settled in the Eight Bars Room around a round table, with tea and Leïla’s cakes. Hortense, Haruka, Sami, and soon Rose-Hélène, who had spotted the academician from afar and had no intention of missing this. Hortense took that day’s newspaper out of her bag. She chose an op-ed, a one-page opinion piece on the place of screens in children’s lives. She gave Haruka three minutes to find a single thing: the author’s thesis.

Haruka read the title. Then the first paragraph. The author said children spent too much time in front of screens. Haruka said that was the thesis. Hortense shook her head. She told her to read the second paragraph, only the first sentence. The sentence began with “Pourtant”. The author explained that this concern, though understandable, was exaggerated. Haruka understood. The thesis wasn’t in the first paragraph. It came after the “pourtant”.

Hortense explained that this was the most classic trap of French argumentative texts. The author often began by presenting the opponents’ view honestly, almost sympathetically. “Some think that…”, “We often hear that…”. Then came the turn: “pourtant”, “cependant”, “or”. The real thesis was there, after the turn. A hurried reader who stopped at the first paragraph understood exactly the opposite of what the author meant.

Rose-Hélène, listening while eating her third honey cake, said it was like Dad when he said: “Yes, of course you can watch TV… but homework first.” The real message came after the “but”. Hortense looked at her very seriously. Then she said it was the best explanation of argumentative structure she had heard in sixty years, and that she would quote it at the Académie. Rose-Hélène asked whether she would get royalties.

Next, Hortense showed Haruka how to find the arguments without reading the whole text. She took a pencil and circled all the connectors in the op-ed: “d’abord”, “ensuite”, “en outre”, “certes”, “mais”, “par conséquent”, “en somme”. When she had finished, the page looked like a map. You could see the whole plan at a glance. Sami said it was like the skeleton of a body: you couldn’t see the flesh, but you could see how everything held together.

Haruka asked what she should do with the words she didn’t know. She had found six in the op-ed. Hortense smiled. She said a lexicographer was the worst person in the world to answer that question, since she had spent her life defining words. But she would give her her mother’s secret anyway. Jeanne Valmont, who never had a dictionary, guessed the meaning of words from the ones around them. She said an unknown word was like a new neighbour: you got to know it by watching who it talked to.

She took Haruka’s first unknown word: “désœuvré”. She asked Haruka to look at the whole sentence. “Les enfants désœuvrés, qui ne savent pas quoi faire après l’école, se tournent vers les écrans.” Haruka reread it. She said “désœuvré” probably meant “who doesn’t know what to do”, since the sentence said so right after. Hortense said that was exactly it. She added: “dés-” as the opposite, and “œuvre” as work. Someone with nothing to do. Haruka wrote the word in her notebook. Without the dictionary.

They did the same with the other five words. Haruka guessed four. The fifth, “gageure”, was too hard; even Sami didn’t know it. Hortense said it didn’t matter, and that if a word was really too hard, it probably wasn’t in the questions. Candidates weren’t asked about words nobody knew. They were asked about ideas. Rose-Hélène asked what “gageure” meant. Hortense said: “Something almost impossible. Like getting Bernard Delorme to be quiet.”

Rose-Hélène burst out laughing. She asked how the academician knew Bernard Delorme. Hortense said she had seen the film “Répondre” four times, and you couldn’t see that film without knowing Bernard Delorme. She added that she dreamt of hearing him play the foghorn. Sami promised to take her to the orchestra one Thursday. Hortense said she hadn’t set foot in an amateur orchestra rehearsal since 1968, and it was high time.

On Sunday, Hortense took the train back to Paris. Haruka and Sami went with her to the station. On the platform she took a worn leather bookmark out of her bag, with embroidered initials: “J. V.”. It was her mother’s. She gave it to Haruka. She said this bookmark had waited sixty years in a dictionary and it was time it travelled through less boring books. Haruka tried to refuse. Hortense got on the train before she could.

Before leaving, Hortense talked to Haruka about the “true or false” questions. She said that was where good readers went wrong most often, because they answered with their intelligence instead of the text. If the text said something foolish, you had to answer according to the foolishness. And justify by copying the exact sentence, in quotation marks, without changing a word. Haruka summed up: “Read between the lines, but justify with the lines.” Hortense said she would steal that sentence.

Hortense also gave her a piece of advice Haruka didn’t expect. She told her to read French newspapers every day for ten minutes, but not to keep informed. To practise finding the thesis. Every morning, one op-ed. Three minutes for the thesis, three for the arguments, three for the unknown words, one for her own opinion. Ten minutes in all. She said that if Haruka did that for a week, she would read twice as fast. Haruka asked whether it had worked for her. Hortense said: “It took me fifty years. But I had no one to tell me.”

On Monday Inès took her to the law faculty library, a large silent room with green lamps. She showed her how she prepared her own exams. First she underlined the keywords in the question. Then she looked in the text not for the same words, but for synonyms. She said examiners almost never reused the exact words of the text in the questions: they rephrased. So you had to look for the idea, not the word. Haruka found that diabolical. Inès said that was law.

The next morning Haruka went down to the café on the corner at the bottom of the rue d’Austerlitz, with Odile’s pencil and a new notebook. She bought the paper. She ordered a coffee, because that café didn’t serve green tea, which was, in her view, France’s only flaw. She looked for the opinion page. She looked at the clock. Ten minutes. She started with the title, then the first sentence of each paragraph, then the connectors. After three minutes she had the thesis.

Haruka had chosen that café by chance, because it was the nearest. She didn’t know that Odile had had her coffee there every morning for forty years. Gérard told her, on the fourth day, when he saw her arrive with the pencil. He recognised it. Odile used to do the newspaper crossword with that pencil, at that same table by the window. She always left half of it for him. She said crosswords, like music, were better done in pairs.

The café owner, a moustached man of about sixty called Gérard, watched her curiously. On the third morning he came over to her table. He asked why she read the paper with a stopwatch. Haruka explained the exam, the thesis, the connectors, the “pourtant”. Gérard listened seriously. Then he said he had been reading that paper for forty years and had never noticed that the op-eds all had the same structure. He said he was going to read everything differently.

Gérard went to fetch something from behind the counter. It was an old chipped white cup with a little blue flower painted on it. Odile’s cup. He hadn’t given it to anyone since she died. He put it in front of Haruka and filled it with coffee. He said that from now on it would be her cup. Haruka said she preferred green tea. Gérard said he would buy some. The next day there was a box of Japanese green tea on the counter.

On the fifth morning, Gérard sat down at Haruka’s table with his own copy of the paper and a kitchen timer. He suggested a contest: whoever found the thesis first won. Haruka won the first day. Gérard won the second, because the op-ed was about football. On the third day they found the thesis at the same time and argued for ten minutes about the wording. The café customers began taking sides. Some asked to play too.

One morning the day’s op-ed was about Lyon’s lime trees. The author, an urban planner, gently mocked those citizens who planted trees everywhere while whistling a waltz. Then, after a well-placed “pourtant”, he acknowledged that the city had never been so green. The op-ed club argued for twenty minutes over whether the author was for or against. Haruka settled it. She said the irony at the start hid admiration. She had found it in the tone. Gérard said she had become more Lyonnaise than he was.

After a week there were six people every morning around Haruka’s table: Gérard, two pensioners, a nurse coming off her night shift, a history student and a delivery driver having his coffee before his round. Each had their own paper and pencil. They looked for the thesis together, discussed the arguments, argued about words. Gérard called it “the op-ed club”. He put a poster in the window. Haruka said she had accidentally founded a club, like Aoi in Kyoto.

After two weeks Haruka noticed something else. She no longer translated. French sentences went straight into her head without passing through Japanese, the way music goes straight into your fingers when you know a piece well. She realised it one morning at the café, reading an op-ed about the Lyon opera: she had understood the thesis before she even knew she was looking for it. She told Gérard. Gérard said he didn’t understand a thing, but he was happy for her.

In the evenings Haruka read with Rose-Hélène. Rose-Hélène was eight and a half and had just started “Le Petit Prince” in French. Haruka had read it in Japanese at ten, then in French at twenty. They read it together, a page each, aloud, sitting in Odile’s armchair. Rose-Hélène stumbled over long words. Haruka stumbled over pronunciation. They helped each other. When they came to a word neither knew, they tried to guess it, as Hortense had taught Haruka.

A few evenings later they read the fox’s sentence everyone knows: “It is the time you have spent on your rose that makes your rose so important.” Rose-Hélène asked what it meant. Haruka thought about it. She said maybe it was like French: she had spent so much time, cried so many times, failed so many mock exams, that now this language had become hers. Rose-Hélène said it was like her name too. She was called Rose. She felt it concerned her.

One evening they reached the passage with the fox, where the fox explains to the little prince what “apprivoiser” means. Rose-Hélène didn’t know the word. Neither did Haruka, in French. They reread the page. The fox said: “It means to create ties.” Rose-Hélène thought for a long time. Then she said it was like the waltz: you whistled, someone answered, and after that you weren’t strangers any more. Haruka said she had never understood that passage better, in Japanese or in French.

Julien had another idea. One Sunday he brought Haruka a cardboard box he kept in a cupboard. Inside were the letters Odile had written him during the years they were neighbours. Little notes slipped under the door, postcards, a long letter written before she died. Julien said they were the best texts he knew for learning to read between the lines. Odile never said things directly. She let you guess.

Haruka’s mother called from Kyoto one evening, worried. She had heard from Aoi that Haruka had failed a mock exam. Haruka reassured her in Japanese. Then she noticed she was putting French words into her Japanese sentences without realising: “en fait”, “du coup”, “bref”. Her mother didn’t understand. Haruka burst out laughing. She told her mother it was a very good sign. French was beginning to seep in everywhere, even into her mother tongue.

Haruka read the letters one by one over several evenings. There was a note from 2027 that said only: “Your piano is a little loud in the evenings. But do carry on with the sonata, I like the second movement.” It took Haruka a long time to understand it wasn’t a complaint. It was a declaration of friendship. Odile wasn’t complaining about the noise: she was telling Julien she listened to him. Haruka said it was the hardest text she had read in French. And the most beautiful.

Amina, for her part, did what she always did: a spreadsheet. It was titled “Haruka’s reading speed” and measured, every evening, how long Haruka took to find the thesis of an op-ed. First evening: eleven minutes. Third: seven. Seventh: four. Tenth: two minutes forty seconds. Amina had drawn a curve. She said she had never seen such a beautiful curve, except Awa’s weight chart. Bertrand pointed out that it wasn’t quite the same thing.

Bertrand suggested harder training. He brought Haruka three Court of Auditors reports, the ones he used to read to Awa before she was born to send her to sleep. Forty-page texts full of figures, endless sentences and technical words. He asked her to find the thesis of the first report. Haruka found it in three minutes, on page six, after a “néanmoins”. Bertrand was impressed. He said that in twenty years’ career he had known magistrates who never found it.

Awa was almost seven months old. She was starting to sit up on her own and grab anything within reach, especially her father’s glasses and her mother’s triangle. She said “ba-ba-ba” all day long, with great conviction. Amina had opened a new column in the “Nous” file, next to “First word”: “Nearly-spoken words”. There were already three: “ba”, “da” and something that vaguely resembled “Haruka”, according to Haruka.

Monday 8 December was the Fête des Lumières. Haruka had never heard of it. Isabelle explained that for more than a hundred and fifty years, every 8 December, the people of Lyon had put candles on their windowsills. The whole city glowed, and millions of visitors came to see the illuminations. That evening Isabelle took out some old coloured-glass candle holders, the ones Odile lit every year. Haruka put them on the windowsill. There were three. She said they were the three notes.

The following Thursday, as promised, Sami took Hortense Valmont to the Thursday orchestra rehearsal. She arrived in her grey suit, with her cane, and sat in the front row next to Leïla. Bernard Delorme, who had been warned, had shaved closely and put on a tie, which he hadn’t done since his daughter’s wedding. He was so intimidated that he hardly spoke all evening. Théo said it was the first time in six years.

Later that evening the whole family went down into the illuminated city. There was a huge crowd. On the façade of Saint-Jean cathedral, artists projected images of light that moved to the rhythm of the music. Climbing back up towards the Croix-Rousse, Rose-Hélène pointed to a window on the third floor of a building. Someone had put three candles there, spaced like notes on a stave. Rose-Hélène whistled. Someone opened the window and answered.

When the waltz came, Hortense listened with extreme attention. At the third verse the orchestra fell silent. On the fifth bar Amina struck her triangle, and Bernard sounded his foghorn. Hortense jumped so hard she nearly fell off her chair. Then she burst out laughing, a young laugh nobody at the Académie had ever heard from her. She told Bernard it was the most extraordinary thing she had heard since 1968. Bernard went bright red. Haruka understood every word.

The night before the mock exam, Haruka couldn’t sleep. She got up and reread Odile’s note from 2027, the one about the piano being a little loud in the evenings. She reread it thinking of everything Hortense had taught her: what the text said, and what it didn’t say. She thought that perhaps the best reading was the one that heard both at once. Then she put Jeanne Valmont’s bookmark on her bedside table, next to Odile’s pencil, and fell asleep.

The second reading mock exam took place on Wednesday 10 December, three days before the real one. Haruka sat in the same room at the Alliance française. She took Odile’s pencil. She skimmed both texts in four minutes. She found the thesis of the argumentative text after the “pourtant” in the second paragraph. She circled the connectors. She guessed three unknown words. She justified every “true or false” with an exact sentence. She had twelve minutes left at the end.

She used those twelve minutes to check. She found one mistake, just one: a “true” that was actually “false”, because the author said “some think that”, not “I think that”. She corrected it. She got twenty-two out of twenty-five. The Alliance française teacher, who had seen her panic three weeks earlier, asked her what had happened. Haruka replied: “I met an academician, a café owner and an eight-year-old girl.”

That same evening Haruka called Hortense in Paris to tell her the result. The academician listened, then said in a perfectly neutral tone: “I’m not in the least surprised.” It took Haruka a moment to understand. Then she laughed. She had recognised the tone. It wasn’t indifference. It was pride, hidden under a dry sentence, French-style. Hortense added that she finally had a pupil who could read between her lines. Haruka said those were the hardest of all.

The next day at the café, Gérard pinned a sheet on the wall next to the coffee machine. It was a photocopy of Haruka’s result: twenty-two out of twenty-five. Underneath he had written in felt-tip: “Founder of the op-ed club”. The six members of the club applauded when she came in. The night nurse had brought croissants. The delivery driver had made a card. The oldest pensioner, a former Latin teacher, said he had never had such a fast pupil in forty years of teaching.

That evening Isabelle packed Haruka’s bag for Saturday with her. Two black pens, in case one ran out. A bottle of water. Her passport and the exam notice. A watch, because phones were forbidden. Odile’s pencil, of course, and Jeanne Valmont’s bookmark, slipped into the exam notice. Isabelle checked each item twice, as Amina would have. Then she said there was still one paper to prepare: the writing. And the oral. Haruka said she knew. She still had two days.

On the evening of Thursday 11 December, two days before the exam, Haruka received a letter from Kyoto. The envelope was written in Japanese, in her grandmother’s fine, careful hand. But inside there was a surprise. The letter was in French. Just three lines, written slowly, with mistakes, in pencil. Her grandmother, at eighty-three, had spent a month writing them, with a Japanese-French dictionary and the help of Aoi, who visited her on Sundays.

It said: “My little Haruka. I not understand French. But I understand you. Saturday, I think of you. Answer.” Haruka read the three lines once, then twice, then ten times. She had read hundreds of texts in French in recent months. Op-eds, articles, novels, Odile’s letters. This was the shortest. It was full of mistakes. It had no thesis, no connectors, no arguments. And it was the only one she had understood completely, first time, without looking for anything between the lines.

That evening Haruka wrote a reply to her grandmother. She wrote it in French, also in three lines, very simply, so her grandmother could read it with her dictionary. She wrote: “My grandmother. She played the three notes very softly, in Odile’s room. On the other side of the landing, someone answered by whistling. Off-key, of course.

Le livre n’a pas dit son dernier mot

We often hear that young people no longer read, that screens have killed the book and that libraries will soon be museums. Admittedly, the time spent in front of phones has never been so long. Yet this alarmist discourse deserves to be nuanced.

First, people have never read as much as today. Messages, articles, forums: we spend our days deciphering words. Reading hasn’t disappeared; it has changed form. It has become faster, more fragmented, but it is everywhere.

Next, media libraries have never been so busy. The one that has just opened in the La Duchère district of Lyon registered a thousand members in a week. Young people come there to work, to meet each other, and also to borrow books.

It could be objected that reading messages is not reading Proust. That is true. But long-form reading, the kind that requires time and silence, has never been the majority practice. It was, yesterday as today, a pleasure that has to be learnt and passed on.

That is where the real issue lies. It is not a matter of mourning an imaginary golden age, but of offering everyone, from childhood, places and moments where reading becomes second nature. Consequently, opening a media library is a bet on the future.
In short, the book has not had its last word. It is simply waiting, as always, for a reader to come and open it. — Op-ed published in the Lyon press, December 2036
